title: Repeated String Match
description: Brute force to optimized: growing the repeated string one copy at a time versus computing the minimum needed length directly.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given two strings a and b, return the minimum number of times a must be repeated (concatenated with itself) so that b becomes a substring of the result. If no number of repetitions works, return -1.

blocks.text: Given two strings a and b, return the minimum number of times a must be repeated (concatenated with itself) so that b becomes a substring of the result. If no number of repetitions works, return -1.

blocks.text: b contains a letter that never appears in a at all, so no number of repetitions of a could ever contain b, giving -1.
It helps to ask exactly how many repeat counts genuinely need to be tried, rather than growing the string one copy at a time and checking after every single one.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Find the Index of the First Occurrence already showed that checking whether a target appears as a substring is itself a solved subproblem; the real question here is how many repeat counts actually need that check run against them at all.

Observation 2: For b to have any chance of being a substring, the repeated string must first be at least as long as b, a fact captured directly by a simple ceiling division of b's length by a's length, with no incremental growth needed to discover it.

Observation 3: Once the repeated string reaches that minimum useful length, a valid match either fits entirely within it, or starts somewhere near the end of it and needs exactly one more copy of a to finish, since a itself is the only unit ever appended.

Observation 4: This means exactly two candidate repeat counts, the minimum length count and one more, are the only ones that could ever succeed, confirmed by tracing a equal to "abcd" and b equal to "cdabcdab" through to the correct answer, 3, without ever needing to try a fourth or fifth repeat.
Recognizing that a length argument bounds the search down to exactly two candidate repeat counts is what replaces growing the string one copy at a time with a direct, constant number of checks.

Repeat a one additional time at a time, and after each repetition, check directly whether b has become a substring of the growing repeated string, stopping once it is found or once the repeated string has grown unreasonably long.

items: Start with one copy of a.
After each repetition, check whether b is now a substring.
Keep repeating and checking until a match is found or a safe upper bound on repetitions is exceeded, at which point return -1.

codes.python:
def repeated_string_match(a, b):
    repeated = a
    count = 1
    while len(repeated) < len(b):
        repeated += a                                           # grow the repeated string one copy at a time
        count += 1
    if b in repeated:
        return count
    repeated += a                                                 # one more copy, in case b spans a boundary
    count += 1
    if b in repeated:
        return count
    return -1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    a = "abcd"
    b = "cdabcdab"
    print(repeated_string_match(a, b))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The repeated string first grows only until it reaches at least the length of b, since anything shorter could never contain it.
One extra copy is appended and checked afterward specifically to catch a match that starts near the end of the minimum length string and spans into the next copy.
Returning -1 only after both of these checks fail correctly signals that no valid repeat count exists at all.

blocks.text: Growing the repeated string just long enough to reach b's length, then checking one extra copy to account for a match that might span the boundary between repeats, correctly covers every possible way b could appear.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((n plus m) times m), where n is the length of a and m is the length of b, since the substring search itself can cost O(length times m) with a naive check, repeated for a couple of candidate lengths.
Space: O(n plus m), for the growing repeated string.

Limitation: the substring search itself, if done naively, can be slower than necessary. Using a more efficient substring search algorithm avoids the worst case quadratic cost of a naive character by character check.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it grows the repeated string one copy at a time and reruns a substring check after every single copy, even though a simple length calculation already tells us where to start.

What computing the minimum length directly fixes: a ceiling division of b's length by a's length gives the exact smallest repeat count worth trying, with no incremental growth needed.

Why one more repeat still needs checking: a valid match could begin partway through the last copy at the minimum length and spill into one additional copy of a.

The core idea: compute the minimum useful repeat count directly, then run an efficient substring search against only that count and the very next one.

Compute the exact minimum number of repeats needed just to make the repeated string at least as long as b, using a simple ceiling division of b's length by a's length. Only two candidate counts ever need checking: that minimum count, and one more than it, since a valid match could span across a repeat boundary. Use an efficient linear time substring search (such as the Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm, or a well optimized built in search) for each of these two checks, instead of an unbounded loop with a naive search.
Compute the minimum needed length directly, then check only two candidate repeat counts using an efficient substring search.

blocks.caption: Optimized: compute the minimum needed length directly, then check just two candidate counts

blocks.text: This works because any repeat count smaller than the minimum length cannot possibly be long enough to contain b at all, and any repeat count larger than one more than the minimum length is unnecessary, since a itself never changes, so a match that does not fit within the minimum length plus one extra copy could never fit no matter how many further copies were appended.

blocks.text:
Time: O(n plus m) using an efficient substring search for each of the two fixed candidate counts.
Space: O(n plus m), for the repeated string built for each candidate.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid growing the string incrementally", think: compute the minimum useful length directly with a ceiling division, then check just that count and one more.
If the interviewer says "why only two candidate counts", think: a match either fits within the minimum length or spills into exactly one more copy, never more.
If the interviewer says "how would you speed up the substring search itself", think: Knuth-Morris-Pratt or a rolling hash, the same techniques from Find the Index of the First Occurrence and Repeated Substring Pattern.

How would you adapt this approach to find the minimum number of repeats needed for b to be a prefix, rather than any substring, of the repeated result?
How would you count the total number of distinct positions where b matches, rather than just finding the minimum repeat count?

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O((n plus m) times m) time, O(n plus m) space. Optimized: O(n plus m) time using an efficient substring search, O(n plus m) space.

items: Pattern: compute the minimum useful repeat count directly from lengths, then check only that count and one more.

Core Idea: a ceiling division of lengths gives the minimum repeat count worth trying, and a valid match can never require more than one additional repeat beyond that, bounding the search to exactly two candidates.
Time: O((n plus m) times m) for the brute force, O(n plus m) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n plus m) for both approaches.
Most Important Observation: a length based argument can bound a search space down to a small constant number of candidates, replacing incremental growth entirely.
Interview Difficulty: the ceiling division insight is the key step; forgetting the "check one more repeat" case is the most common mistake even among those who find the main idea.
One line memory trick: compute the minimum length with ceiling division, then check that count and one more, nothing else.
